extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic and philosophy; readers seeking an introductory, rigorous account of reasoning, language, and evidential standards
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory analytic treatment of logic focused on the role of language: what logic is, its scope and limits, and the classification and proper use of names and propositions as instruments of reasoning and evidence-estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of logic (aim and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the science of the operations of the understanding which are subservient to the estimation of evidence: both the process of advancing from known truths to unknown, and all other intellectual operations in so far as auxiliary to this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes Naming, Definition, and Classification because these operations help marshal facts and make evidence and conclusions permanent and accessible; excludes more elementary mental processes (Conception, Memory, etc.) that have no special connection to evidence. The practical object is to analyze Reasoning/Inference and to frame rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of evidence to prove propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic as practical art — limit of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A logician should analyze mental operations only so far as is requisite for ascertaining the difference between a correct and an incorrect performance of those processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not carry analysis beyond the point at which any inaccuracy would become visible; avoid overly metaphysical or anatomical decompositions that are irrelevant to practical discrimination of right and wrong in inference. Analytic depth is determined by the needs of logical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that improvements in logical notions advance science
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress in the more difficult sciences is usually preceded or accompanied by corresponding improvements in the notions and principles of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that limitations in a field may reflect inadequate logical notions; therefore refining logical principles is a legitimate route to advancing empirical or theoretical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of logic to other sciences and metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the sovereign judge when any science begins to draw inferences from evidence; its relation to metaphysics is no different than its relation to other sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a discipline moves from introspection to evidence-based inferences, logic must assess whether those inferences are well grounded; do not treat metaphysics as exempt from logical scrutiny when it uses evidence and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of commencing with an analysis of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is one of the principal instruments of thought; any imperfection in it or in its use is liable to confuse the process of thinking and destroy confidence in results, so an inquiry into language is a necessary preliminary to logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before teaching methods of philosophizing, teach pupils the meaning and right use of words to prevent inference errors; language analysis guards against distorted 'glasses' that would mislead subsequent logical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions as the form of answers and objects of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Every possible question's answer must be contained in a proposition; whatever can be object of belief or disbelief, when put into words, assumes the form of a proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To know what questions can be asked and answered, survey and analyze propositions; recognize that truth and error lie in propositions (true/false propositions) and that analyzing their forms reveals the space of intelligible inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a proposition (subject, predicate, copula)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition consists of three parts: the Subject (the thing spoken of), the Predicate (the attribute affirmed or denied), and the Copula (the sign denoting affirmation or denial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'Gold is yellow' — 'gold' is subject, 'yellow' predicate, 'is' copula. Understanding these parts is foundational for subsequent logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief requires two objects (subject and predicate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest act of belief supposes two objects—two names; one object alone ('the sun') does not call for belief until coupled with another (e.g., 'the sun exists').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that assertions bring distinct concepts together (e.g., 'the sun' + 'existence'); without this pairing there is nothing to affirm or deny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names are names of things, not merely of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word is used to express belief, it is a name of the thing itself and not merely a name of our idea of the thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'the sun is the cause of day' asserts a relation between things, not between ideas; treat names as standing for the objects about which we assert facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between names and parts of names (categorematic vs syncategorematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words are names (categorematic terms) able to stand as subject or predicate; others are only parts of names (syncategorematic), such as particles, inflected pronouns, and some adjectives when not used predicatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether a word can be the subject or predicate of a proposition by itself; if not (except when referring to the mere word form), treat it as syncategorematic. Avoid treating non-name words as independent logical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-worded names and the predication test
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of words may constitute a single name; determine whether a sequence of words is one name by predicating of it and observing whether only one assertion is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'John Nokes, who was the mayor of the town, died yesterday' counts as one name in subject position; contrast 'John Nokes and the mayor of the town died' which makes two assertions. Use predication to decide name-unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of names: general vs individual (singular)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is capable of being truly affirmed, in the same sense, of each of an indefinite number of things; an individual name is only truly affirmed of one thing (in the same sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'man' is general (applies equally to many individuals); 'John' is individual because it doesn't convey qualities common to many. Use this distinction when forming general propositions versus singular assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of names: general vs collective
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name can be predicated of each individual of a multitude; a collective name cannot be predicated of individual members but only of the whole (e.g., 'the 76th regiment' is collective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse collective with general: 'a regiment' is both collective and general (applies to many regiments); 'the 76th regiment' is collective but not general with respect to its soldiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of names: concrete vs abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: A concrete name stands for a thing (object); an abstract name stands for an attribute of a thing (e.g., 'John' vs 'whiteness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the classical usage (abstract = name of an attribute, concrete = name of an object). Be aware of modern looser usages that call all products of abstraction 'abstract'; preserve the distinction for clarity in logical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: On adjectives versus abstract nouns (usage guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives (e.g., 'white') are names of things having an attribute, whereas abstract nouns (e.g., 'whiteness') are names of the attribute itself; in predication we typically use the adjective to denote objects possessing a quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When saying 'snow is white' we predicate an object has a color; when saying 'whiteness' we mean the color itself. Prefer interpreting words by their principal use in predication to decide whether they name attributes or objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methodology: begin analysis from ordinary language distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by recognizing the distinctions made by ordinary language; use names as a clue to the things to bring before inquiry the distinctions recognized by all inquirers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose theoretical taxonomy at the outset; start from the catalogue of distinctions present in common usage and then abridge or revise only when close examination shows them non-fundamental. This avoids missing distinctions recognized across inquirers.
